parsed.explanation: The combined regime pairs a deeply hostile society with an imminent identity-criminalisation statute. The 2026 bill (passed, awaiting assent widely expected to be signed) makes identifying as transgender or cross-dressing punishable by up to three years, adds advocacy offences and a duty to report — a near-universal exposure for any outed or outable visitor, though not yet in force and with no enforcement record against visitors. Existing law, documented mob justice against perceived LGBT people, state security raids closing LGBTQ centres, no anti-discrimination protection, no legal recognition and effectively no working remedy place this in the High Risk band. Severity stops at short imprisonment (no execution or documented custody torture for visitors), but probability of hostile discovery and thin recourse are high.

entry_documents.exposure: No trans-specific entry or airport screening rule is documented. Once the bill is assented to, identification/cross-dressing offences could surface at any document check; application to short-term visitors is explicitly unresolved.
entry_documents.protection: No documented entry denial or marker-specific screening practice; nothing in the sources shows visitors targeted at the border.
entry_documents.interaction: Document-presentation mismatch → identification offence → duty to report by staff/officials → police involvement; the chain is plausible but not documented as applied to visitors.

investigation_detention_custody.exposure: Pending bill criminalises identifying as transgender (up to 3 years) with a duty to report; existing 'unnatural carnal knowledge' law and documented mob justice supply additional levers once discovery occurs.
investigation_detention_custody.protection: Bill not yet assented to; supreme court review deferred but not resolved. No documented arrest of a trans visitor. No prison-placement or custody-abuse record for trans detainees appears in the sources.
investigation_detention_custody.interaction: Discovery by any actor triggers reporting duty and police involvement; judicial review only becomes available after signature, leaving present legal status contested.

federal_state_facilities.exposure: No national prison placement rule, trans special unit, or facility (bathroom/ward) rule for visitors is documented in any source.

care_services.exposure: No visitor-facing care denial rule is documented. Conversion therapy and family rejection are recorded but are resident/youth-facing, not traveller exposures.
care_services.protection: Medical bodies condemning conversion therapy; a paralegal initiative exists — both resident-sphere and thin.
care_services.interaction: An emergency care disclosure could interact with the pending identification offence and the duty-to-report provision; not documented in practice.

threat_framing_law_enforcement.exposure: State and political elites frame LGBT identity as a threat: bill criminalises identity itself; national security raided and closed an LGBTQ office after local/religious opposition; religious pressure drove 2026 passage.
threat_framing_law_enforcement.protection: An international organisation called for veto; petitioners' lawyers exploring further options — no demonstrated effect.
threat_framing_law_enforcement.interaction: Official threat-framing licenses mob justice and reporting duties, converting social hostility into state process.

minors_guardians.exposure: For a travelling family: pending identity offence plus duty to report could implicate a gender-nonconforming minor or a parent. Resident-facing conversion therapy and family rejection show the social climate a visiting minor would enter.
minors_guardians.protection: No documented minor-specific protection or exemption. Dated 2017 poll showing 55% support for legal gender change is a weak climate signal only.
minors_guardians.interaction: A child's disclosure or presentation could trigger reporting by school, host or community actors into the same criminal pipeline.

street_violence_police_response.exposure: Mob justice against perceived LGBT people is documented; community organisations operate secretly or on the dark web after forced closures. Evidence of police conduct is dated (2017–2018 reports).
street_violence_police_response.protection: Resilient underground community; no documented pattern of police protection for trans victims, and no anti-discrimination or hate-crime statute.
street_violence_police_response.interaction: A foreigner as visible outsider plus thin police protection heightens exposure; foreign status is not shown to shield.

remedies_unknowns.exposure: Supreme court deferred review until assent; no anti-discrimination protection; community infrastructure closed rather than sheltered; enforcement of the 2026 bill against visitors is an open question.
remedies_unknowns.protection: Human-rights-trained paralegals defend LGBTQ people in court; constitutional challenge options remain after signature.
remedies_unknowns.interaction: Paper challenge routes exist but the state has already shut down the organisations that would support a visitor; effective recourse for a short-term traveller is undocumented.

anchor_checks.comparison: Lower than 0.15-B: that anchor documents routine post-inspection detention, cells with assaults, withheld medical care and delayed habeas hearings. This dossier documents no entry-bar, no visitor detention record and no custody-abuse evidence — the identity offence is imminent but unenforceable until assent.

Similar but somewhat worse: 0.25-C combines birth-sex prison housing with cross-dressing arrests in administrative buildings. Here the pending bill criminalises transgender identity itself nationwide with a reporting duty, backed by documented mob justice and state closure of LGBTQ bodies — broader exposure, though still capped at ~3 years and not yet signed.

Materially lower than 0.45-A: that anchor assumes routine checkpoint exposure with uncommon prosecutions and a narrow anti-discrimination claim available. This dossier has no functioning protection, documented mob violence and elite consensus driving imminent identity criminalisation — harsher law-in-progress plus worse social record.

parsed.synthesis: Law and society are aligned against the traveller. The operative regime today combines an existing morality statute, documented mob justice, official closure of LGBTQ institutions and no anti-discrimination or recognition machinery, with an identity-criminalisation bill awaiting assent that the president has signalled she will sign. Judicial review is frozen until signature, so no protection operates now. There is no documented visitor-specific enforcement, no entry screening rule and no custody-violence record — which keeps this out of the 0.05–0.15 tier where execution, systematic detention or documented torture appear. But an outed visitor faces a plausible path from social discovery through a reporting duty to imprisonment, against a backdrop of societal hostility and near-total absence of remedy, placing the rating at the boundary of Severe and High Risk.
